trial_name: CRYOSTAT-2 — Early and Empirical High-Dose Cryoprecipitate for Hemorrhage After Traumatic Injury (2023)
citation: Davenport R, Curry N, Fox EE, et al; CRYOSTAT-2 Investigators. Early and Empirical High-Dose Cryoprecipitate for Hemorrhage After Traumatic Injury: The CRYOSTAT-2 Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2023;330(19):1882-1891.
trial_type: Pragmatic, parallel-group, randomised, open-label, multicentre superiority trial
one_liner: Empirical early high-dose cryoprecipitate added to standard major hemorrhage protocols did not reduce 28-day mortality in adults with active traumatic hemorrhage.

pico.population: Adult trauma patients (age >=16) with active hemorrhage triggering a major hemorrhage protocol, SBP <90 mm Hg, receiving >=1 unit blood component within 3 hours of injury.
pico.intervention: Empirical high-dose cryoprecipitate (3 pools, ~6 g fibrinogen equivalent) targeted within 90 minutes of hospital arrival and within 3 hours of injury, plus standard care.
pico.comparison: Standard care major hemorrhage protocol alone (balanced component therapy, with cryoprecipitate permitted if protocol/clinician triggered).

background.existing_knowledge: Severe traumatic hemorrhage causes early preventable death. Fibrinogen is often the first coagulation factor to reach critically low levels, leading to increased bleeding and mortality.
background.knowledge_gap: Cryoprecipitate is traditionally delivered late due to preparation logistics, and the clinical efficacy of empirical early replacement remains uncertain.
background.hypothesis: Empirical early high-dose cryoprecipitate delivered within a pragmatic window improves 28-day mortality compared with standard major hemorrhage protocols.

methods.design: Pragmatic, parallel-group, open-label, multicentre RCT stratified by centre across 26 major trauma centres in the UK and US.
methods.setting: 26 major trauma centres (UK and US); emergency department and early in-hospital resuscitation.

inclusion: Injured adults (>=16 years or judged adult)
Active hemorrhage with activation of major hemorrhage protocol
Systolic blood pressure <90 mm Hg at any time
Receipt of >=1 unit of any blood component
exclusion: Injuries considered incompatible with life by trauma team leader

methods.intervention: Empirical high-dose cryoprecipitate (3 pools, ~6 g fibrinogen equivalent) added to standard care, targeting administration within 90 minutes of arrival and within 3 hours of injury.
methods.comparison: Standard care major hemorrhage protocol with balanced component therapy. Standard cryoprecipitate allowed if triggered by local protocol or clinician judgment.
methods.sample_size_power: Planned 1600 patients; powered for 7% absolute reduction in 28-day mortality (26% to 19%) with 90% power at 2-sided 5% alpha using group sequential O'Brien-Fleming design.
methods.primary_outcome: 28-day all-cause mortality (intention-to-treat analysis using mixed logistic regression adjusting for centre).
secondary_outcomes: Mortality at 6 hours, 24 hours, and 12 months
Cryoprecipitate pools transfused in first 24 hours
Total blood products and crystalloids in first 24 hours
Cumulative incidence of thrombotic events at day 28
methods.follow_up: Primary outcome at 28 days; long-term survival to 12 months; functional/QoL outcomes at hospital discharge and follow-up.

headline_bullets: Early high-dose cryoprecipitate delivered cryoprecipitate faster (median 68 vs 120 min) and increased exposure (median 3 vs 0 pools in 24 hours).
No significant reduction in 28-day all-cause mortality (25.3% vs 26.1%, OR 0.96).
No differences detected in 6-hour, 24-hour, or 12-month mortality, total blood product use, ventilator days, or thrombotic events.
Prespecified subgroup analysis showed higher 28-day mortality with early cryoprecipitate in penetrating trauma (16.2% vs 10.0%, OR 1.74, interaction P=0.004).

outcomes_table.note: RBC median 5 vs 5 units; plasma median 4 vs 4 units
Higher volume in early cryo group
Quality of life at discharge unchanged

safety: Cumulative thrombotic events at day 28: 12.7% (95% CI 10.1–15.6) vs 12.9% (95% CI 10.2–15.8), absolute difference -0.2% (95% CI -4.1 to 3.7, P=0.89).
Venous thromboembolism: 6.9% in intervention vs 7.1% in standard care.
Arterial thrombotic events: 3.3% in intervention vs 3.2% in standard care.
Increased 28-day mortality observed in penetrating trauma subgroup (16.2% vs 10.0%, OR 1.74, 95% CI 1.20–2.51).

domains.notes: Centre-stratified computer-generated randomisation using sequential sealed envelopes.
Unblinded without placebo; primary mortality endpoint is objective, but clinical co-interventions and subjective secondary outcomes could be influenced.
1604 randomised (799 vs 805); 73 (4.6%) excluded from primary analysis due to consent withdrawal or missing outcome (39 vs 34), leaving 1531 analysed (760 vs 771).
Only 54% (434/799) received intervention within protocol delivery constraints; 32% (256/795) of standard care received cryoprecipitate in first 24h.
Groups balanced for ISS (median 29 vs 29), SBP <90 mm Hg (32% vs 34%), and TXA use (79% vs 80%); slight imbalance in severe head injury (head AIS >=4: 24% vs 29%).

internal_validity.verdict: Internal validity is moderate due to open-label design, protocol non-adherence (46% non-compliant), 4.6% post-randomisation exclusions, and standard care contamination.

domains.notes: Representative of adult major trauma patients with hypotensive active hemorrhage in mature trauma systems.

Applicable to major trauma centers operating component transfusion protocols; less generalisable where cryoprecipitate delivery is slow/absent or where fibrinogen concentrate or prehospital whole blood strategies dominate.

external_validity.verdict: External validity is moderate-to-good for mature major trauma centers with standard component therapy protocols.

strengths: Large pragmatic multicentre trial across 26 major trauma centres in UK and US
Pragmatic design evaluating a real-world systems-level intervention
Objective primary endpoint with long-term follow-up to 12 months
Achieved significant separation in timing (68 vs 120 min) and total cryoprecipitate dose
limitations: High rate of protocol delivery deviation (only 54% received intervention per protocol constraints)
Substantial contamination with cryoprecipitate in standard care arm (32%)
Loss of 4.6% of randomised cohort post-randomisation
Lack of patient selection using viscoelastic or laboratory hypofibrinogenemia criteria

critical_appraisal.summary: CRYOSTAT-2 provides strong pragmatic evidence that universal empirical high-dose cryoprecipitate does not improve survival in major trauma, though implementation delays and control-arm contamination weaken causal precision.
strengths: Large sample size (n=1604) in major trauma networks
Robust objective mortality endpoint at 28 days and 12 months
weaknesses: 32% crossover cryoprecipitate use in standard care

sections.authors_conclusion: In adults with traumatic injury and active hemorrhage requiring major hemorrhage protocols, empirical early high-dose cryoprecipitate did not reduce 28-day all-cause mortality compared with standard care.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: Do not routinely administer empirical early high-dose cryoprecipitate to all unselected trauma activations triggering major hemorrhage protocols.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Adult trauma activations with severe bleeding and hypotension managed with major hemorrhage protocols.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: Fibrinogen replacement is ineffective; targeted replacement for documented hypofibrinogenemia remains indicated.
implementation_caveats: Universal empirical dosing increases transfusion volume and costs without clinical benefit
Real-world delivery delays limit the ability to achieve immediate early fibrinogen replacement with cryoprecipitate
Concern for potential harm in penetrating trauma requires cautious evaluation

controversies.notes: Only 54% of patients received cryoprecipitate within protocol time constraints, and 32% of standard care received cryoprecipitate within 24 hours, making this a comparison of timing/intensity rather than binary exposure.
A statistically significant interaction (P=0.004) showed higher 28-day mortality in penetrating trauma (16.2% vs 10.0%, OR 1.74), though mechanistic plausibility remains uncertain.
Broad unselected administration without viscoelastic or laboratory confirmation of hypofibrinogenemia likely diluted potential treatment benefits.

unresolved_questions: Does targeted fibrinogen replacement based on viscoelastic or rapid point-of-care testing improve survival?
Is the mortality signal in penetrating trauma a true biological harm or a false-positive subgroup finding?
Can prehospital administration or fibrinogen concentrates overcome logistics delays to demonstrate early benefit?

numbers_to_remember: Penetrating trauma mortality: 16.2% vs 10.0% (OR 1.74, interaction p=0.004)
Delivery time to cryo: 68 min vs 120 min (54% protocol compliance)
quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: Do not give routine empirical cryoprecipitate in severe trauma resuscitation; reserve fibrinogen replacement for targeted, laboratory-guided administration.
